name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SEMICONDUCTOR_ELECTRONICS_MCQ_Q01 - Thermal generation and movement of holes

questiontext.text:
In an intrinsic semiconductor such as silicon at a temperature \( T > 0\text{ K} \), thermal excitation leads to conduction through both free electrons and holes. Consider the microscopic events involved in the thermal generation and apparent movement of a hole through the crystal lattice:

(I) Thermal energy breaks a covalent bond in the crystal lattice, releasing a free conduction electron.
(II) A vacancy with an effective positive charge, known as a hole, is created at the site of the broken bond.
(III) A valence electron in a neighbouring intact covalent bond acquires energy and jumps into the vacant site.
(IV) The original vacancy is filled, and a new vacancy is formed at the neighbouring bond site from which the electron hopped.
(V) Under an external applied electric field, continuous sequential hopping of bound valence electrons creates a macroscopic hole current moving towards the negative potential.

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these events?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In an intrinsic semiconductor, electrical conduction involves two independent charge carriers: free electrons in the conduction band and holes in the valence band. A hole represents an electron deficiency (vacancy) in a covalent bond that behaves as an apparent mobile particle with an effective positive electronic charge \( +q \).

Step 2: Sequential Analysis of Physical Events
The microscopic process unfolds in the following physical order:
First, at finite temperatures (\( T > 0\text{ K} \)), thermal energy imparted to the lattice vibrates the silicon atoms, occasionally supplying enough energy to break a covalent bond and release a conduction electron.
Second, the departure of the thermally excited electron leaves behind an unoccupied covalent bond with an unneutralised positive core charge, forming a hole at that specific lattice site.
Third, an adjacent bound valence electron in a neighboring bond can transition into this unoccupied site without becoming a free conduction electron.
Fourth, once this valence electron occupies the initial vacant site, the initial bond becomes intact, but a new vacancy is simultaneously produced at the donor bond site, resulting in the apparent displacement of the hole.
Fifth, when an external electric field is applied, these successive jumps of bound valence electrons occur preferentially towards the positive potential, causing the apparent vacancy (hole) to migrate towards the negative potential and constitute a steady hole current.

Step 3: Verification of Sequence Logic
A hole cannot move before it is generated, and valence electron hopping into a site requires a pre-existing vacancy. Furthermore, directed macroscopic current is the cumulative result of directional hopping under an applied field. Hence, the logical progression flows naturally from initial thermal ionisation to lattice-site hopping, followed by apparent motion, and finally field-driven drift.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is: Thermal bond breaking and electron release → Creation of a vacancy (hole) → Valence electron jump from an adjacent bond → Apparent movement of the hole to the adjacent site → Macroscopic hole drift under an applied electric field.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SEMICONDUCTOR_ELECTRONICS_MCQ_Q02 - Stages in formation of pn junction

questiontext.text:
When a p-type semiconductor wafer is partially transformed to synthesize an integrated metallurgical junction with an n-type semiconductor, several physical processes occur to establish an unbiased p-n junction. Arrange the following stages in their correct logical sequence:

(I) Due to concentration gradients, majority holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side and majority electrons diffuse from the n-side to the p-side, setting up a diffusion current.
(II) Diffusing carriers recombine near the interface, leaving behind immobile ionised donor cores on the n-side and immobile ionised acceptor cores on the p-side, creating a space-charge depletion region.
(III) An internal barrier electric field builds up across the depletion region, directed from the positive space-charge (n-side) towards the negative space-charge (p-side).
(IV) The electric field sweeps minority carriers across the junction, initiating a drift current directed opposite to the diffusion current.
(V) As the space-charge layer widens, the drift current increases until it equals the diffusion current, establishing dynamic equilibrium with zero net current.

Which of the following gives the correct chronological order?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The formation of a p-n junction is governed by two opposing carrier transport mechanisms: diffusion due to carrier concentration gradients, and drift driven by the induced internal space-charge electric field.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Analysis of Junction Formation
1. Initially, a steep concentration gradient exists across the metallurgical junction because hole concentration is much greater on the p-side and electron concentration is much greater on the n-side. Consequently, majority holes diffuse from p to n and majority electrons diffuse from n to p.
2. As electrons diffuse across to the p-side, they leave uncompensated positive donor ions fixed in the n-lattice. Similarly, holes diffusing to the n-side leave uncompensated negative acceptor ions fixed in the p-lattice. This creates a region stripped of mobile carriers called the depletion layer.
3. The presence of positive ions on the n-edge and negative ions on the p-edge produces an internal electric field pointing from n to p.
4. This internal electric field exerts forces on minority carriers that enter the depletion zone (electrons on the p-side and holes on the n-side), driving them across the boundary and generating a drift current in the opposite direction to diffusion current.
5. As diffusion continues, the depletion region widens, intensifying the electric field and increasing the drift current. Eventually, the drift current precisely balances the diffusion current, leading to an equilibrium barrier potential \( V_0 \) with zero net current across the terminal leads.

Step 3: Verification of Sequence Logic
Diffusion is the primary driving mechanism that uncovers immobile ion cores. These immobile cores are the direct source of the electric field. In turn, the electric field is the prerequisite for carrier drift, which grows until equilibrium balance is attained.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is: Diffusion of majority charge carriers → Space-charge depletion layer formation → Generation of internal electric field → Initiation of minority carrier drift → Attainment of dynamic equilibrium with equal diffusion and drift currents.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SEMICONDUCTOR_ELECTRONICS_MCQ_Q03 - Operation of rectifier with capacitor filter

questiontext.text:
In a full-wave rectifier circuit equipped with a parallel capacitor input filter across a load resistor \( R_L \), arrange the following stages in their correct chronological sequence during one complete steady-state operational cycle:

(I) The rising input alternating voltage applied to the conducting diode exceeds the residual voltage across the capacitor, forward-biasing the diode.
(II) The forward-biased diode conducts current heavily, charging the capacitor up to the peak voltage of the rectified sinusoid.
(III) The rectified input sinusoid peaks and starts falling, causing the diode to become reverse-biased as its anode potential drops below the capacitor potential.
(IV) With the diode cut off, the capacitor discharges stored charge through the load resistor \( R_L \) with a rate governed by the time constant \( R_L C \), maintaining the output voltage.
(V) In the subsequent half-cycle, the voltage across the secondary winding reverses and rises until it exceeds the falling voltage across the capacitor, switching the alternate diode on.

Which of the following represents the correct sequence?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A capacitor input filter smoothens rectified ac pulsations into a near-steady dc voltage. The diode conducts only during short intervals when the input ac transformer secondary voltage exceeds the capacitor voltage; during the remainder of the cycle, the diode remains reverse-biased and the capacitor sustains load current by discharging through \( R_L \).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working of the Filter Cycle
1. At the beginning of the conduction period, the rectified ac voltage rising towards its peak reaches and then exceeds the decaying voltage retained across the capacitor. This makes the diode anode more positive than its cathode, establishing forward bias.
2. Once forward biased, the diode acts as a low-resistance path, allowing current to flow into both the load and the capacitor, rapidly charging the capacitor until the voltage reaches the peak rectified value \( V_{\text{peak}} \).
3. Immediately after the input wave passes through its peak, the input voltage drops below \( V_{\text{peak}} \). Because the capacitor holds the peak voltage, the cathode of the diode is at a higher potential than its anode, reverse-biasing the diode and turning it off.
4. During this cutoff period, the diode does not conduct. The capacitor delivers energy to the load resistor \( R_L \), discharging slowly with an exponential rate determined by the time constant \( \tau = R_L C \).
5. In the next half-cycle, the opposite half of the centre-tapped secondary produces an increasing positive voltage at the alternate diode. When this new pulse exceeds the declining capacitor voltage, the alternate diode is forward-biased, re-initiating the charging cycle.

Step 3: Verification of Operational Cycle
Charging to peak must precede discharging, and diode cutoff naturally occurs the instant the sinusoidal input decreases below the capacitor's peak voltage. Conduction in the alternate half-cycle can only occur once the alternate secondary voltage overcomes the remaining voltage on the capacitor.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is: Input voltage exceeding capacitor voltage → Diode conduction and capacitor charging to peak voltage → Input voltage falling below peak causing diode cutoff → Capacitor discharging through load resistor → Input voltage in next half-cycle rising to recharge capacitor.
